Senses.Explanation: The two daily gruel-and-rice meals are the monastery’s fixed meal-times. Zhaozhou says that during forty years he had no mixed use of mind apart from these meals; later masters quote, challenge, and institutionalize that formula, including the right of ordained residents to receive them. Zhaozhou’s saying defines the recurring formula: apart from the two gruel-and-rice meals, he had no mixed use of mind. Lamp and instruction records repeatedly quote it. Wuzhun Shifan asks where Zhaozhou fell outside the two meals, then counters that when gruel comes one eats gruel and when rice comes one eats rice. Gaofeng Yuanmiao uses the same phrase autobiographically when saying that for nearly three years he did not mount the cushion outside the two meal-times. Qianshan Shengren gives the phrase an institutional edge: before ordination, he says, even the two daily meals count as stolen food. The headword names actual scheduled meals before it carries any quoted contrast.

Senses.Explanation: Mixing mud and blending water pictures two substances losing a clean boundary. Shishuang Chuyuan places it first in a three-part warning: understanding at the first phrase is ‘mixing mud and blending water,’ at the second ‘binding oneself without a rope,’ and at the third ‘landing with all four edges on the ground.’ Huqiu Shaolong also gives the phrase as a direct answer to ‘What is the true source of the great way?’ and pairs it with a place where wind cannot enter. Baofu Congzhan contrasts black and white remaining indistinct with recognition that comes too late, which he calls mixing mud and blending water. These speakers put the same image to different uses; the phrase itself does not supply one fixed favorable or unfavorable verdict.

Yuanwu Keqin explains the inherited image in the Blue Cliff Record: a clam from the Han River floats at the water's surface at mid-autumn, opens to the moonlight, and forms a pearl. His Record of Fogu's Beat-the-Rhythm Sections states the same relation more briefly: on a mid-autumn night, the clam takes in moonlight to produce a pearl. Yuanwu says both of Zhimen's answers use the mid-autumn idea, then adds that the old master's meaning is not located in the clam or rabbit. Cishou Huaishen likewise repeats the paired images and explicitly places them at mid-autumn.
